hints: Focus on this phrase: lowers the partial pressure of oxygen at which haemoglobin is 50% saturated. If you need LESS oxygen around to still get half loaded, does haemoglobin grab oxygen more easily or less easily?

Remember the rule for the dissociation curve: if haemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly, it reaches high saturation at a lower partial pressure, so the whole S-shaped curve moves toward lower values on the x-axis.
walkthrough:
**Understand what P50 means**

Think of 50% saturation as the halfway point of loading. The partial pressure needed to get there is called the P50.

Here the mutation lowers that value, so haemoglobin becomes 50% loaded even when there is very little oxygen around.

**Link a lower P50 to affinity**

If you can pick up oxygen easily even at low partial pressure, your affinity (attraction) for oxygen must be high.

So lower P50 = higher affinity. It holds on more tightly and loads more readily.

**Link higher affinity to curve position**

On an oxygen dissociation curve, the x-axis is partial pressure of oxygen and the y-axis is % saturation.

Higher affinity means high saturation is reached sooner, at lower partial pressures, so the curve shifts to the left. That matches higher affinity and shift to the left.

options.A: Correct. A lower P50 means haemoglobin loads oxygen more easily, so affinity is higher and the curve shifts to the left.
options.B: Affinity is indeed higher, but a higher affinity always shifts the curve to the left, not to the right.
options.C: A lower P50 means higher, not lower, affinity, even though a left shift is correct for high affinity.
options.D: Both parts are reversed. Lower affinity would need a higher P50 and would shift the curve to the right.
